title: Climate Change Forces Hydrological Regime Shifts in Australian Wetlands
content:
Abstract

Wetlands provide crucial biodiversity benefits and ecosystem services but are at risk from changing hydrological regimes under climate change. Understanding likely future changes in wetland hydrology will help mitigate impacts and guide adaptation strategies for high-value sites. We used satellite-based observations of wetland inundation to calibrate conceptual runoff models modified to represent wetland storage dynamics across 34,890 wetlands in the state of Victoria, Australia. Wetlands across Victoria feature a range of hydrologic regimes, from permanent waterbodies to highly episodic systems that inundate only every few years. We assessed future climate-driven changes in seven wetland ecohydrological metrics used to inform wetland water regime classification for a subset of 11,660 high performing wetland models. By 2075 in a high emissions scenario (SSP3-7.0), up to 90% of wetlands are projected to change their hydrological regime classification, and the statewide average annual maximum inundated area might reduce by 60%, relative to 1988–2022. The biggest risk is to permanent wetlands, where even under a moderate emissions scenario (SSP2-4.5) and median climate change projections, over two thirds could transition to seasonal or intermittent systems by 2075. Wetlands with extremely rare inundation and thus low biodiversity and ecosystem benefits are projected to increase nine-fold under SSP3-7.0. These projected hydrological regime shifts imply risks to wetland-dependent species and ecosystem services. Our findings provide a large-scale and transferable quantitative assessment of climate change impacts on wetland hydrology, highlighting critical vulnerabilities from a drying climate.
